title: You can play a theremin without touching it
body: A theremin turns hand movements in the air into music, with **no keys or strings to touch**. The player's hands interact with electric fields around two antennas, changing the instrument's electronic circuits. One antenna controls pitch, meaning how high or low a note sounds, while the other controls volume. Moving through the space around them lets the performer shape a continuous tone.

left.label: Pitch antenna
left.text: The upright antenna controls how high or low the sound is.

right.label: Volume antenna
right.text: The horizontal antenna controls how loud or soft the sound is.

slides.heading: How a theremin makes a note

steps.label: One hand moves near the upright antenna
Its electric field shifts the circuit
The pitch rises or falls with the hand
The other hand sets the volume

slides.heading: The air becomes the interface
slides.text: The instrument responds to the position of the player's hands. Electronics generate the sound; the performer controls it through movement.

slides.heading: This is not a recent invention
slides.text: The Science Museum Group holds an RCA theremin manufactured in 1929. Playing music without touching the instrument has a history stretching back nearly a century.

slides.question: What does the theremin’s upright antenna control?
slides.explanation: The upright antenna sets how high or low the note is, while the horizontal one controls volume. The player’s hands interact with the electric fields around each.

source.label: Science Museum Group: RCA Theremin, USA, 1929
